title: Adnan Sami Blasts Bollywood's Remix Addiction: 'Corporates Are Scared to Experiment'
excerpt: The singer-composer says music labels have flipped the original-to-remix ratio from 80:20 to 20:80, starving a generation of its own songs.
body:
• Singer-composer Adnan Sami says the ratio of original songs to remixes in Bollywood has flipped from 80:20 to 20:80, blaming corporate risk aversion.
  • Speaking on the Game Changers podcast, Sami argued that audiences are starving for original music but labels keep serving remixes because they are "safe."
  • He compared the trend to feeding someone plain rice and claiming they love it — when they were never offered biryani.
  • Sami also defended music directors, saying no composer ever dreamed of making remixes and the blame lies with labels forcing the practice.

Adnan Sami has taken aim at the Bollywood music industry's deepening dependence on remixed songs, calling it a symptom of corporate fear rather than audience demand. In a wide-ranging conversation on the Game Changers podcast with interviewer Komal Nahta, the singer-composer argued that record labels have effectively starved listeners of original content while conveniently blaming the shortfall on public taste.

The 80:20 Flip

"It is always lovely to revive an old song. In my opinion, the ratio should be 80-20, with 20 being the remixed songs. That's how it was before. But now, it's 20-80," Sami told Nahta, breaking into laughter at the absurdity of the reversal.

The root cause, he said, comes down to one word: khauff — fear. "The corporates are scared to experiment. It is happening even in cinemas. Remakes are attempted, sequels are made; even prequels are planned," Sami said, drawing a parallel between Bollywood's music and film industries. He pointed to Hollywood's own franchise fatigue, noting how DC exhausted the Batman character before spinning off into Joker, and how Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, despite being based on an ancient text already adapted in 1954, has crossed nearly $1.5 billion at the global box office.

"When you ask record labels why they keep making remixes, they reply, 'Because the public wants it.' But if a man is hungry and you present him with plain rice, he'll eat it eagerly. That doesn't mean he wanted plain rice — you just never served him biryani."

— Adnan Sami

A Generation Without Its Own Songs

Beyond the commercial calculus, Sami raised a deeper cultural concern. "Every generation calls certain songs their own. My father used to say a particular song was from his era. I would feel the same for 'Chura Liya Hai.' The ones who grew up in the 90s would feel a sense of belonging for the songs of Aashiqui," he said. "But which song would this generation consider their own? After all, you have mostly presented recreated versions to them."

The observation strikes at a chord familiar to diaspora audiences, for whom Bollywood music often serves as a primary link to cultural identity. The remixed versions of classics from the 1970s, 80s and 90s retain iconic hooks and choruses while swapping out original stanzas — a formula Sami described as keeping the mukhda and changing the antara.

Don't Blame the Composers

Sami was emphatic about where accountability lies. "I can give you in writing that no music director ever dreamed as a child that he would grow up and work on remixes. So, don't blame them. Blame those who make them do it by force," he said, according to Bollywood Hungama.

The statement positions the issue as one of structural pressure rather than creative failure. Composers working under label contracts have little say in whether their next assignment is an original composition or a reworked version of a 1990s hit, according to Sami. The economic logic is straightforward: a familiar melody carries built-in recognition, reducing marketing risk for labels already operating on thin margins in a streaming-dominated market.

A Broader Pattern

Sami's critique arrives at a moment when Bollywood's creative ecosystem faces questions from multiple directions. Box office returns increasingly favor sequels and franchise entries, while original stories struggle for screen space. The music industry mirrors this pattern, with remix-heavy soundtracks dominating playlists even as independent artists and non-film music gain traction on streaming platforms.

For now, Sami — who earned widespread recognition with chart-topping tracks in the early 2000s — recently released his single Ishq Tamasha through Zee Music Company, a pop-rock track that underscores his own commitment to original work.
nri_angle: Bollywood music serves as a cultural anchor for diaspora Indians, and the remix trend threatens to dilute the generational connection to original Hindi film songs.
author: Diaspora Desk
